title: Lotus Sutra 3
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk highlights the importance of personal motivation in Buddhist practice, particularly in Soto Zen. Rather than trying to achieve enlightenment for the benefit of others, individuals should focus on their own suffering and dissatisfaction as a catalyst for spiritual growth. This approach allows compassion and universal benefit to emerge naturally from one's own awakening, rather than being forced or artificial. By grounding practice in personal experience, individuals can develop a more authentic and spontaneous path to liberation.

sentences.text: Among the several really important themes of the Lotus Sutra is one we've already seen quite a bit and repeated throughout: the difference between the arhats, the earlier practitioners who learned about suffering, the end of suffering and the gradual path toward the end of suffering, and the practitioners of the Lotus Sutra, who understand the world cosmically and non-dualistically to be already awakened and unlimited in terms of our usual space-time concepts.
The contrast between those two kinds of practitioners is one of the key themes of the Lotus Sutra.
On the one hand, historically, it's dueling doctrines, I suppose, but there's something deeper to it than that, I think.
When you think about one's own path of practice, it does make sense, and it is really true, that the path of practice begins with one's own suffering one way or the other.
You either are in anguish and you absolutely can't go on without practice, or maybe you just feel like life isn't quite what it should be, somehow.
I want life to be deeper, stronger, something.
Something in you wants to practice, so you start practicing.
You're not aspiring to save all sentient beings, anything like that.
You just feel like you want to practice, and you have a desire that practice would make a difference in your life, and you hope that it will.
That seems to be really the proper and strongest motivation.
When somebody comes and says, "I'm showing up today to practice and I want to save all sentient beings and I want to get enlightened and I want to…", you wonder about that.
But if somebody comes and says, "Well, life is hard and I want to find a way to cope," you think, oh yes, that's much better.

There's much more chance that that person will actually see this through and stay with it for a while, because the person is fairly grounded in their motivation and clear about what they're doing and what they're looking for.

But then you go down that road of your own benefit, your own suffering, your own desire for some peace, and you find that in order to alleviate one's own suffering and to find peace for oneself, the road widens out and ends up being a path of compassion, a path of universal benefit for everyone, a path of loving kindness.

After a while you don't even notice, it doesn't even make any difference anymore, what difference it makes to you in your life or how it works in your life, because that is how it makes a difference in your life, that is how it works in your life: the opening that you feel in practice to practice for and with others.
So I think that's exactly what happens through the motivation of suffering and the end of suffering, desire for relief, desire for peace, deeper understanding of life or whatever it is.
Walking down that road, the path opens up and becomes wider and deeper, and the faith in this limitless world that the Lotus Sutra is constantly depicting becomes stronger and stronger.

Another way I was thinking about this today, another way to look at this, is to think about the human capacity for endless desire and therefore endless dissatisfaction, and also endless idealism and endless imagination.
Really our minds are just like the Lotus Sutra, boundless in their capacity to invent all sorts of things that aren't.
Other creatures live in the world that is.

We live in the world that is and also in the world that could be or that should be, that we would like it to be, and our capacity to construct such worlds is far greater than any worlds that ever could be.

No matter how many worlds could be, there's always more of them that could be, and so our dissatisfaction is really without bound, as infinite as the many mutas of kothis of Buddha realms the Lotus Sutra describes.
So many mutas of kothis of possibilities of dissatisfaction and desire do we human beings have.

So the Lotus Sutra, I think, recognizes this infinite human capacity, which is an imaginative, conceptual capacity for creativity in a way, but creativity that usually turns against us, in other words creativity that makes us dissatisfied with what is.
The Lotus Sutra taps into that endless creativity, flips it and opens it up for Dharma.
If we were to start practice with that, if that were the beginning point of practice, I think practice would become very chaotic and spinning all over the place.
So we can't really tap into that at first.
It's better to just do a simple grounded practice like sitting, walking, standing, breathing, bowing.

But eventually that very practice of sitting, standing, walking, breathing, bowing engages the whole of the imagination, the whole of this conceptual capacity, and then when we're grounded in our basic fundamental stability, all that can be engaged without being destabilized.
So these are some ways that I thought of today to help us understand the extravagance of the Lotus Sutra in this constant dialectic between the way of the arhats and the way of the Lotus Sutra.
Of course, I think we've already seen in the Sutra that the Buddha is saying that the arhats are not exactly wrong or limited.
In fact, all along, as he says, they've been, without even knowing it, walking the path of the Lotus Sutra.
Well, I think we got as far as the fifth chapter.

We did some of the famous parables, the parable of the burning house, which we went into at length, and then in the last chapter the parable of the medicinal herbs, which likens the Dharma to a rain cloud equally sending rain on all the plants.
The plants are completely different, each one from the other, but the rain falls equally on them all and gives them the moisture they need so that each one can grow in its own way.

This is a metaphor for the Dharma and expedient means: each sentient being is unique and needs a different Dharma, and yet the Dharma is at the same time one, but just activates in people's lives uniquely.
The sixth chapter is called, in the Watson translation, Bestowal of Prophecy.
You remember that earlier in the Sutra, Shariputra, one of the arhats, expressed a little dismay that he had been left out of this great, enthusiastic prediction of Buddhahood.
Everybody was becoming Buddhas right and left, and he was thinking, gee, I'm only an arhat, too bad I didn't get in on this great stuff.
And the Buddha said, oh no, no, no, it's all right, you have a prediction as well.
So in chapter six, the Buddha makes a prediction on behalf of Mahakasyapa.
He says that Mahakasyapa will in future times be a Buddha, and his realm will look like this, and he will have this kind of retinue, and so forth and so on.
Then he makes a prediction for Sabhuti, Katyayana, and these are all the names of historical disciples of Buddha, Magdalyayana.
All of them he gives Buddha names and Buddha retinue and so on.
So that chapter is easy to summarize: a bunch of predictions for more arhats.
Next comes chapter seven.
This is the famous parable of the Phantom City.

As I said before, the Lotus Sutra is known for its parables, and this one is as famous as any of the other ones, but it's preceded by about a 20-page-long story, which is very far out, a kind of preamble to the parable, which doesn't appear until something like page 135, and the chapter starts on page 117.
So for the first 17 pages, this is [unclear: "a men's story"] of this Buddha whose name is Great Universal Wisdom Excellence.
Now, Shakyamuni Buddha in the present, seated in the Lotus Sutra-giving assembly, is telling the story of this Buddha, Great Universal Wisdom Excellence.
How long ago did this Buddha live?
*Well, now monks, since that Buddha passed into extinction, a very great, a very long time has passed.

Suppose, for example, that someone took all the earth particles in the thousand million fold world and ground them up to make ink powder, and as he passed through the thousand lands of the east, he dropped one grain of the ink powder, no bigger in size than a speck of dust.*
I guess in a thousand lands, one speck of dust of ink powder, the quantity of which is equal to the amount of earth particles in the thousand million fold world.
So he's got a lot of particles there, and he's going a thousand lands and dropping one, and another thousand and dropping another.
*So suppose he went on this way until he had finished dropping all the grains of ink made from the earth particles.
Now what is your opinion?

Do you think that with regard to those lands, the masters of calculation or the disciples of the masters of calculation would be able to determine the number of lands that have been visited in the process, or would they not?*
*That would be impossible, world-honored one.*
That would be a lot of lands that couldn't be calculated.
*Now monks, suppose that one should take the earth of all the lands this man had passed through, whether he dropped a grain of ink there or not, and should pound all those lands into dust.
And suppose that one particle of dust would represent one kalpa,* one glacial age, geological age.
*The kalpas that had elapsed since that Buddha entered extinction would still*
